paragraphs.text: Zevachim 116b — “One verse says, 'David gave Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight,' while another says, 'David bought the threshing floor and the cattle for fifty shekels of silver.' How can both be maintained? He collected fifty from each tribe, making six hundred. Rebbi said in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dostai: The cattle, wood and place of the altar cost fifty; the entire Temple site cost six hundred.” Rav Tzadok follows the first resolution, which makes the purchase a contribution shared by all twelve tribes. The Gemara also preserves a second resolution; its fifty and six hundred refer to different parts of the purchase.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Bo 39b — “At first it says, 'He smelled the fragrance of his garments.' When he perceived it, he said, 'See, the fragrance of my son,' knowing that the matter depended upon him, for on his account the fragrance arose: 'like the fragrance of a field that Hashem has blessed.' How did Yitzchak know the fragrance of a field that Hashem had blessed? ... It is written, 'Yitzchak went out to meditate in the field toward evening.' Did he have no house or other place to pray? Rather, that field was the one Avraham bought beside the cave. When Yitzchak entered it, he saw the Shechinah resting upon it, and sublime, holy fragrances arose. He therefore prayed there and established it as his place of prayer.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Tazria 4 — “The beginning of creation was that the Shechinah dwell among the lower beings; after the sin, the place of the Mikdash remained and was called ‘field,’ and so too after the actual destruction.” Rav Tzadok there gives the reason behind the name used here: “field” is the Mikdash site as holiness not yet, or no longer, built, which is why it links Adam, Machpelah and the Mikdash.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 88a — “Rabbi Elazar said: What is meant by 'Many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us ascend Hashem's mountain, to the house of the God of Yaakov'? Is He the God of Yaakov and not the God of Avraham and Yitzchak? Rather, it is unlike Avraham, in whose case 'mountain' is written: 'As it will be said today: On Hashem's mountain He will be seen'; and unlike Yitzchak, in whose case 'field' is written: 'Yitzchak went out to meditate in the field.' Rather, it is like Yaakov, who called it a house: 'He called the name of that place Beis El.'” The Gemara identifies the patriarchal places of prayer with the future Temple. Rav Tzadok relates its 'field' to the field beside Machpelah in the Zohar; that identification is his synthesis of the sources.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 22:7 — “Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in Rabbi Levi's name: Both took land and both took movable property. Over what, then, did they dispute? One said, 'The Temple will be built in my territory,' and the other said, 'The Temple will be built in my territory.' For it says, 'When they were in the field,' and 'field' means the Temple, as in 'Zion shall be plowed as a field.' From this came 'Kayin rose against his brother Hevel.'”

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 14:8 — “'From the earth': Rabbi Berechyah and Rabbi Chelbo said in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman's name: He was created from the place of his atonement, as it says, 'You shall make Me an altar of earth.' The Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'I am creating him from the place of his atonement; would that he endure!'” The Midrash makes the possibility of repair part of man's very creation. Rav Tzadok extends this to Adam's return to the altar after the sin and to the body's eventual entry through Machpelah.

From there He had taken him, and there He returned him, to the place from which he had been taken. ... From which place had He taken him? From the place of the Temple, as it says, 'To work the earth from which he had been taken.'” This passage explicitly supplies the location that Rav Tzadok reads into the verse: Adam returns to Moriah and the Temple site.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Beis HaBechirah 2:2 — “There is a tradition held by all that the place where David and Shlomo built the altar at Aravnah's threshing floor is the place where Avraham built the altar and bound Yitzchak upon it. It is the place where Noach built an altar when he left the ark; it is the altar upon which Kayin and Hevel offered. There Adam offered a sacrifice when he was created, and from there he was created. The Sages said: Adam was created from the place of his atonement.”

paragraphs.text: Genesis 3:19 — “By the sweat of your face shall you eat bread, until you return to the earth, for from it you were taken: you are dust, and to dust shall you return.” Rav Tzadok reasons from the earth of Adam's creation to the place of his burial. The verse itself states the return to earth; the relation between the altar and Machpelah is the argument developed here.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 58a; Rashbam, s.v. Rabbi Benaah — “Rabbi Benaah was marking burial caves. ... When he reached Adam's cave, a heavenly voice came forth and said: 'You have looked at the likeness of My image; do not look at My image itself.' He answered, 'But I must mark the cave!' He was told: 'The dimensions of the outer chamber are the same as those of the inner chamber.' ... Rabbi Benaah said: 'I looked at his two heels, and they were like two disks of the sun.' All people beside Sarah are like an ape beside a human; Sarah beside Chavah is like an ape beside a human; Chavah beside Adam is like an ape beside a human; Adam beside the Shechinah is like an ape beside a human.” Rashbam explains that Rabbi Benaah measured the caves inside and marked their boundaries outside with lime, so that people carrying ritually pure objects would recognize the place of impurity and avoid passing over a grave. This explains the relevance of the episode to Rav Tzadok's concern about burial impurity.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 20 — “He sat and reflected in his heart: 'You will return me to death, the appointed house for every living being.' Adam said, 'While I am still in the world, I shall build myself a lodging for my resting place outside Mount Moriah.' He hewed and built himself a resting place. Adam said: 'The tablets will be written by the Holy One's finger, and the Jordan's waters will flee before them. My body He formed with both His hands, and into my nostrils He breathed the spirit of His mouth. After my death, might they take me and my bones and make them an object of idolatry? Rather, I shall deepen my coffin below the cave and within the cave.' It is therefore called the Cave of Machpelah, for it is doubled. There lie Adam and Chavah, Avraham and Sarah, Yitzchak and Rivkah, Yaakov and Leah; it is called Kiryas Arba because four couples were buried there.” The Midrash explains concealment of Adam's grave as protection against worship of his body. Rav Tzadok's account of impurity and the cave's sanctity draws on this burial tradition together with the preceding sources.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Chayei Sarah 127b — “Moreover, he prayed every day and would go out to that field, from which sublime fragrances arose. He saw light emerging from the cave and prayed there; there the Holy One, blessed be He, spoke with him. For this reason he sought to acquire it: his longing was continually for that place. If you ask why he had not sought it until now, it was so that they would not take notice of him while he had no need of it. Now that he needed it, he said: 'The time has come to seek it.'”

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Bo 5 — “'The fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field that Hashem has blessed,' for sublime, holy fragrances rose there. Fragrance indicates that the defect has been repaired and that he has attained the quality of tzaddik. ... This is the sublime fragrance that Avraham perceived from the Cave of Machpelah through the light of Adam, who was buried there. There is also a sublime, holy fragrance: the balsam described in the Zohar as the lofty, hidden and concealed chamber.” This is the precise internal passage invoked to distinguish Avraham's 'sublime fragrances' from the 'sublime, holy fragrances' associated with Yitzchak. The English renders selected clauses of the original passage; the intervening discussion explains purity through fear of Heaven.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Chayei Sarah 123b, Tosefta — “Rabbi Abba said: Come and see what is written: 'Avraham listened to Efron, and Avraham weighed out to Efron the silver.' This is the great longing of those worlds and yearnings. 'Four hundred shekels of silver': four hundred worlds, enjoyments and yearnings. 'Current with the merchant': Rav Nachman said that the soul passes through all the gates of heaven and the heavenly Jerusalem, and no one prevents it.” The text plays on kesef, silver, and kisuf, longing. Rav Tzadok interprets its four hundred worlds through the completeness of the four worlds, rather than as worldly material pleasures.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 12:7 — “Hashem's words are pure words, silver refined in an earthen crucible, purified sevenfold.” The verse supplies the image of sevenfold purification. The numerical comparison of seven times seven with seven times ten is Rav Tzadok's explanation here.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Bereishis 47b — “'They were completed': the works above and the works below were completed. 'The heavens and the earth'—above and below. Rabbi Shimon said: The work and craftsmanship of the Written Torah, and the work and craftsmanship of the Oral Torah. 'And all their hosts'—these are the Torah's particulars, its facets: seventy facets of Torah. 'They were completed'—they were established and perfected in one another. Heaven and earth are particular and general; 'all their hosts' are the Torah's mysteries and its laws of purity and impurity.” The exact cited folio places Torah's seventy facets within the completion of the Written and Oral Torah in one another. Rav Tzadok further interprets seventy as seven qualities each comprising ten.

paragraphs.text: Uktzin 3:12 — “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: In the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will cause every tzaddik to inherit three hundred and ten worlds, as it says: 'To bequeath substance to those who love Me, and I shall fill their treasuries.'” The word yesh has the numerical value 310. The Mishnah cites both halves of the verse; Rav Tzadok distinguishes love and fear within them to account for the additional ninety.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 12 — “The four hundred worlds are not desires of this world, but the enjoyment of the radiance of the Shechinah, the lofty apprehensions that will be attained in the World to Come. ... 'Their treasuries' means the treasury of fear of Heaven, which is their own treasury. ... The letter tzaddi is the tzaddik, Yosef's quality, the ninth attribute; nine times ten, when it includes the aspect of the Congregation of Israel, is ninety. 'I shall fill their treasuries' thus means ninety worlds attained through fear, Yosef's quality, as he said: 'I fear God.' ... Together with the 310 worlds that Hashem bequeaths in His kindness to those who love Him, these make four hundred worlds.” The earlier maamar supplies the otherwise compressed calculation: the reward associated with love is 310, and the treasury of fear contributes ninety. These are Rav Tzadok's distinctions within the Mishnah's proof verse.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Chayei Sarah 129a — “When he had grown old and entered the sublime degrees as was fitting, it says, 'Avraham was old'; then he 'came into the days'—those sublime days, the days known in the mystery of faith. 'Hashem blessed Avraham with all': from there issue all blessings and all goodness.” The Zohar explains the 'days' as sublime degrees. The specification that the tenth trial integrated all ten qualities is developed by Rav Tzadok, rather than explicitly stated in this quoted Zohar passage.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah 2 — “After the Akeidah, when Avraham Avinu was completed in all ten middos… then he bought the field of Machpelah… and the light emerging from the cave is from the first light.” Rav Tzadok there ties the timing of the purchase to this same completion, and identifies the cave’s light with the fivefold “light” of creation that this maamar later connects to the five Chumashim.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Mishpatim 94b — “When a person is born, he is given a nefesh from the animal aspect, from the side of purity, from those called the holy Ofanim. If he merits more, he is given a ruach from the holy Chayos; if he merits more, a neshamah from the Throne. ... If he merits more, he is given a nefesh in the manner of Atzilus, from the only daughter, called the King's daughter. If he merits more, he is given a ruach of Atzilus from the middle pillar and is called a son of the Holy One. If he merits more, he is given a neshamah from Father and Mother. ... If he merits more, he is given the Divine Name with its letters in full—yod, heh, vav, heh—which is Adam, in the manner of the supernal Atzilus; he is called the image of his Master.” The repeated 'if he merits more' describes successive gifts of higher soul levels. Rav Tzadok relates this ascending structure to completeness throughout the four worlds.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Vayakhel 204a — “What is Shabbat? If you say it is because of cessation, as it is written, ‘For on it He ceased,’ that is fitting. But the mystery of the matter is: When this point rises and light shines, then she is crowned with the patriarchs. Once she is crowned with the patriarchs, she joins and unites with them to become one, and all is called Shabbat. Shabbat—shin, bat: shin is the mystery of the three patriarchs, who unite with the only daughter, and she is crowned with them. ... All is one.”

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 79a — “Three signs distinguish this nation: they are merciful, bashful, and doers of kindness. Merciful, as it is written, 'He will give you mercy, and have mercy upon you and multiply you'; bashful, as it is written, 'So that His fear may be upon your faces'; doers of kindness, as it is written, 'For I have known him, that he may command his children and his household after him.' Whoever has these three signs is fit to join this nation.” The Gemara lists the three traits and their scriptural supports. The assignment of kindness to Avraham, bashfulness and fear to Yitzchak, and mercy to Yaakov is Rav Tzadok's patriarchal interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 20a — “It was taught: 'So that His fear may be upon your faces'—this is bashfulness. 'So that you do not sin' teaches that bashfulness leads to fear of sin. From here they said: It is a good sign in a person that he is bashful. Others say: A person who feels shame will not readily sin; one who lacks a sense of shame is known not to have had his ancestors stand at Mount Sinai.” The connection between shame and fear of sin explains why Rav Tzadok places bashfulness under Yitzchak's quality of fear.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Zohar, Terumah, section 6, beginning “Patach Rabbi Shimon bereisha” — “Whoever wishes to engage in a commandment, and through it to attach himself to the Holy One, blessed be He, must not undertake it emptily and without cost. Rather, a person must undertake it properly, according to his strength.... Torah study is available to whoever wishes to attain it; seeking knowledge of the Holy One is available without any payment. But Divine service that is fulfilled through an act may not be obtained emptily and without cost: through that act one draws upon oneself a spirit of holiness only with full payment.... A holy spirit comes through full payment, very great effort, purification of oneself and one’s dwelling, and the willingness of one’s heart and soul. Would that a person might succeed in having it dwell with him.”

This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s explanation of the remembered merit of Avraham’s payment: the silver expresses his eagerness to acquire a place of holiness, rather than serving merely as the price recorded in a transaction.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 58:8 — “Rabbi Elazar said: How much ink is poured out, how many pens are broken, to write 'the children of Ches'! 'The children of Ches' is written ten times, corresponding to the Ten Commandments, to teach that whoever establishes a tzaddik's purchase is as though he fulfills the Ten Commandments. Rabbi Yudan said: 'The children of Barzillai' is written five times, corresponding to the five books of Torah, to teach that whoever feeds a morsel to a tzaddik is as though he fulfills the five books of Torah.” Both comparisons occur together in the Midrash. Their differing numbers are the question that Rav Tzadok proceeds to explain.

paragraphs.text: Yefeh Toar on Bereishis Rabbah 58, s.v. Ke’ilu mekayem aseres hadibros — “'As though he fulfills the Ten Commandments': This is the Sages' manner in several places: one who assists a Torah scholar is considered as though he fulfilled the entire Torah, because through his help the scholar can occupy himself with Torah. There is therefore no question why the Torah alluded to ten regarding the children of Ches and to five regarding the children of Barzillai, for one does not raise objections against allusions.” This is the precise comment summarized in the manuscript. The checked digital edition places its heading under 'As though he fulfills the Ten Commandments'; Rav Tzadok nevertheless seeks meaning in the different numbers.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 3:5 — “Rabbi Simon said: Light is written here five times, corresponding to the five books of Torah. 'God said: Let there be light' corresponds to Bereishis, in which the Holy One occupied Himself with creating His world. 'There was light' corresponds to Shemos, in which Israel emerged from darkness into light. 'God saw the light, that it was good' corresponds to Vayikra, filled with many laws. 'God separated the light from the darkness' corresponds to Bamidbar, which distinguishes those who left Egypt from those who entered the Land. 'God called the light day' corresponds to Mishneh Torah, filled with many laws.”

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 14:9; Proverbs 20:27 — “Five names were given to it: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, yechidah, chayah. Nefesh is the blood, as it says, 'The blood is the nefesh.' Ruach ascends and descends, as it says, 'Who knows the ruach of human beings that ascends upward?' Neshamah is the disposition, as people say, 'A good disposition.' Chayah: all the limbs die, yet it lives within the body. Yechidah: the limbs come in pairs, while it is unique within the body.” The Midrash supplies the five names; Rav Tzadok arranges them as ascending levels and relates them to the five expressions of light. Proverbs 20:27 reads: 'A person's soul is Hashem's lamp, searching all the chambers of the belly.'

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 92:4 — “'They took the gift ... Yosef saw Binyamin with them ... and prepare': Prepare refers only to Shabbos, as it says, 'On the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring.' This shows that Yosef observed Shabbos before it was given.” This is the passage supporting the identification of Yosef's meal as a Shabbos meal. The checked digital edition numbers it 92:4; the manuscript cites 92:7.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Mikeitz 6 — “'Binyamin's portion increased fivefold beyond the portions of them all': The expression 'increased' suggests that it increased of itself. ... The principal intention of Yosef was to feed them the remnants of his Shabbos meal, which was truly the King's meal; the remnants had the power to bring holiness into all the tribes. ... The Shechinah rested upon Israel in Binyamin's territory in five places. ... Although Yosef introduced holiness into all the tribes, in Binyamin the holiness increased fivefold, for the Shechinah rested in his portion in five places. The number five indicates completeness, for there are five levels of the soul: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah.” The cited earlier maamar explicitly joins Binyamin's fivefold portion to the five places of the Shechinah and to the five soul levels. It presents alternate ways of counting the places according to the opinions in Zevachim 118b.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 7 — “Since Binyamin, through his holiness, attained all five holinesses of Shabbos—as it says, 'Binyamin's portion increased,' increasing of itself—there is no place here for jealousy, for he truly possessed what they had not attained. Consequently there is likewise no jealousy over Yosef's giving him five changes of garments and giving the others one, for he had attained what required the tzaddik to shed upon him the encompassing light in the five holinesses of Shabbos. ... Corresponding to these are the five levels of the soul: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah and yechidah.” This companion reference explains the fivefold gift as the outer expression of a holiness Binyamin had already attained. It makes explicit why Rav Tzadok treats the five portions as soul nourishment rather than merely a larger meal.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 56a — “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonasan's name: Whoever says that David sinned is simply mistaken, for it says, 'David conducted himself wisely in all his ways, and Hashem was with him.' Is it possible that sin came into his hand while the Shechinah was with him? What, then, is the meaning of 'Why have you despised Hashem's word, to do evil'? He sought to do so but did not do it. ... 'You struck Uriah the Chittite with the sword': You should have judged him before the Sanhedrin, but did not. 'You took his wife to be your wife': You had a valid marriage with her.” The Gemara's defense of David addresses the legal character of the episode while retaining criticism of his conduct. Rav Tzadok invokes that defense when describing Barzillai's support of David during exile.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Introduction 17a, Patach Eliyahu — “You brought forth ten arrangements, which we call ten sefiros, through which to govern concealed worlds that are not revealed and worlds that are revealed. ... In this arrangement they are called: Chesed, the right arm; Gevurah, the left arm; Tiferes, the body; Netzach and Hod, the two legs; Yesod, the end of the body, the sign of the holy covenant; Malchus, the mouth, which we call the Oral Torah. Chochmah is the brain, inward thought; Binah is the heart, through which the heart understands. ... The supernal Kesser is the crown of kingship. Of it it is said: 'Declaring the end from the beginning.' It is the skull of the tefillin; within it is the Name spelled Yod, Heh, Vav, Heh, which is the path of emanation.” The passage gives the ten sefiros the form of a complete human configuration. That embodied completeness explains why Rav Tzadok associates the purchase of a burial place for the body with ten, rather than the five soul levels nourished through food.
